title: State v. Payne
description: Whether a trial court has jurisdiction to realign a defendant's sentences from consecutive to concurrent after vacating death sentences due to an intellectual disability determination, with the State arguing against such jurisdiction and the defendant arguing for it.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that once a criminal judgment is final, a trial court can only modify it if a statute explicitly grants that authority, and no statute granted authority to realign Payne's sentences after his intellectual disability determination.
defendant_argument: Payne contended that trial courts have broad discretion over sentencing matters and retained this discretion to impose concurrent sentences after his intellectual disability determination, as no statute expressly forbade it.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the conversion of death sentences to life imprisonment for Pervis Payne due to intellectual disability but vacated the trial court's order to realign his sentences to be served concurrently, ruling that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to modify the final judgment in that respect.

title: Wygant v. Lee (formerly Moore v. Lee)
description: Whether Ms. Hunt, a voter, has standing to challenge the constitutionality of her own voting district due to unconstitutional misnumbering, with the plaintiff arguing she has standing due to representational harm and the defendant arguing she lacks standing as her injury is not actual or imminent.
plaintiff_argument: Ms. Hunt argues she has standing because she was placed into an unconstitutionally misnumbered voting district, causing her representational harm and diluting her political power, which constitutes an actual and imminent injury.
defendant_argument: The defendant (and the majority opinion) argues Ms. Hunt lacks standing because her alleged injury is not actual or imminent, her voting opportunity was accelerated, not delayed, and her claim does not involve vote dilution or gerrymandering.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Ms. Hunt does not have standing to challenge the constitutionality of her voting district.

title: State v. Green
description: Whether a drug-sniffing canine's positive alert, which cannot distinguish between legal hemp and illegal marijuana, can still contribute to probable cause for a vehicle search under the totality of the circumstances.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that a positive alert from a certified drug-detection dog still establishes probable cause to search a car, despite the legal status of hemp, especially when viewed as part of the totality of the circumstances.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that a canine sniff cannot provide probable cause because the dog cannot differentiate between legal hemp and illegal marijuana, making its alert unreliable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Criminal Appeals' judgment, concluding that law enforcement had probable cause to search the vehicle and reinstating the indictments against the defendant.

title: McKay v. State
description: Whether Public Chapter 182, which transfers the representation of the State in capital collateral review proceedings from the locally elected district attorney to the Attorney General, violates Article VI, § 5 of the Tennessee Constitution. The plaintiff argues it infringes upon the district attorney's constitutional authority, while the defendant argues it is a valid legislative act defining the duties of state attorneys.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Larry McKay, and DA Mulroy argued that Public Chapter 182 violated Article VI, § 5 of the Tennessee Constitution by impeding the inherent discretion and authority of the locally elected district attorney general, whose constitutional duty to "attend and prosecute" criminal cases extends to collateral review proceedings.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Tennessee (represented by the Attorney General), argued that Article VI, § 5 does not prohibit the delegation of trial court collateral defense authority to the Attorney General, as the district attorney's prosecutorial discretion ends upon a final judgment of conviction, and collateral review proceedings are not criminal prosecutions.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's order, holding that Public Chapter 182 does not violate Article VI, § 5 of the Tennessee Constitution and that the Attorney General is not disqualified from representing the State in capital collateral review proceedings.

title: Smith v. BlueCross BlueShield of Tennessee
description: Whether the right to petition in the Tennessee Constitution is enforceable against private employers and can serve as a public policy exception to the employment-at-will doctrine, with the plaintiff arguing it should protect employees communicating with legislators, and the defendant arguing it applies only to government actions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that her termination violated Tennessee's public policy, based on her constitutional right to petition, and that this right should protect employees communicating with legislators, even against private employers, as it is fundamental for a functioning free republic.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the plaintiff's termination was lawful under the employment-at-will doctrine, and that the right to petition protects citizens from abusive government action, not private employer-employee relationships, thus not forming a basis for a public policy exception.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, affirming the trial court's dismissal of the plaintiff's complaint, holding that the right to petition in the Tennessee Constitution is enforceable only against governmental entities, not private parties.

title: Rainwaters v. Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency
description: Whether Tennessee Code Annotated subsections 70-1-305(1) and (7), which authorize Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency (TWRA) officers to enter private property without warrants or consent to enforce wildlife laws, are constitutional both facially and as applied.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the statute authorizing warrantless entries onto private property is unconstitutional on its face and as applied, violating Article I, Section 7 of the Tennessee Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the statute is facially constitutional because it can be applied to wild waste lands, and constitutional as applied because TWRA officers only enter private property when they believe hunting activity is occurring, making the searches reasonable.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that Tennessee Code Annotated subsections 70-1-305(1) and (7) are facially constitutional but unconstitutional as applied to the plaintiffs, and affirmed the award of nominal damages.

title: Dotson v. State
description: Whether the provisions of Tennessee Supreme Court Rule 13 for prior approval review of expert funding requests are constitutional as applied, whether the Petitioner was unconstitutionally denied appellate review of the denial of expert funds, and whether the Petitioner was deprived of a full and fair post-conviction hearing due to the denial of expert funds.
plaintiff_argument: The Petitioner argued that Rule 13's prior approval provisions are unconstitutional, that he was unconstitutionally denied appellate review of expert funds, and that he was deprived of a full and fair post-conviction hearing due to the denial of expert funds.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Rule 13 provisions are constitutional, the Petitioner was not unconstitutionally denied appellate review, and he received a full and fair post-conviction hearing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgments of the post-conviction court and the Court of Criminal Appeals, holding that Rule 13 provisions are constitutional, the Petitioner was not unconstitutionally denied appellate review, and he received a full and fair post-conviction hearing.

title: Falls v. Goins
description: Whether Ernest Falls' right to vote in Tennessee was automatically restored upon receiving clemency in Virginia, or if he must also comply with additional Tennessee statutory requirements for re-enfranchisement.
plaintiff_argument: Ernest Falls argued that his right to vote in Tennessee was automatically restored when Virginia granted him clemency, as per Tennessee Code Annotated section 2-19-143(3).
defendant_argument: The State Officials argued that Mr. Falls must comply with additional requirements under Tennessee Code Annotated section 40-29-202, such as paying court costs, restitution, and child support, to regain his voting rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that Ernest Falls must comply with both Tennessee Code Annotated sections 2-19-143(3) and 40-29-202 to regain his right to vote in Tennessee.

title: Metropolitan Government of Nashville & Davidson County v. Tennessee Department of Education
description: Whether the Education Savings Account Pilot Program (ESA Act) violates the Home Rule Amendment of the Tennessee Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The ESA Act violates the Home Rule Amendment because it is local in form or effect, applicable to the counties in their governmental capacity, and does not require local approval, thereby infringing on local control of local affairs and requiring them to fund LEAs at the same level despite students leaving for private schools.
defendant_argument: The ESA Act does not violate the Home Rule Amendment because it only regulates Local Education Agencies (LEAs), which are distinct from county governments, and therefore is not 'applicable to' the counties themselves in the meaning of the Home Rule Amendment.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that the ESA Act does not implicate the Home Rule Amendment and is therefore not unconstitutional on that basis, remanding the case for dismissal of that claim.
